title: MATKP Static Information
bodyHtml:
Where is adipose tissue found? 

Adipose tissue is found throughout the body in different depots. While many depots have orthologs across all mammals, there are also some important species-specific differences in depot size, type, and location. Consider the hump of the camel, for example, which is a major adipose depot for that species, but which has no obvious counterpart in other mammals. 

Depots can be classified in several ways. Many authors emphasize a distinction between subcutaneous (under the skin and outside of the major body cavities) vs. visceral depots (which includes fat in the peritoneal and thoracic cavities). A large amount of mammalian adipose tissue falls within one of these categories, but not all. As one example, fat in the bone marrow cannot be classified as subcutaneous or visceral. Depots can also be classified by their content of thermogenic adipocytes, identified as “white” or “brown”. Here again, many depots contain a mixture of brown and white adipocytes, which may vary even within the same depot, depending on the ambient temperature.

What cell types make up adipose tissue? 

The major parenchymal cell of adipose tissue is the adipocyte, which make up roughly half of the cells in the fat pad. A major distinction among adipocytes is whether they are thermogenic or not, i.e., whether they have the capacity to generate heat from the inefficient burning of calories. There are two major types of thermogenic adipocytes: brown and beige. Both are rich in mitochondria and express proteins that enable calorie wasting and heat generation, such as uncoupling protein 1 (UCP-1). Brown adipocytes are present at all times under all conditions (although they may not be activated), and comprise distinct depots in rodents. In contrast, beige adipocytes reside within predominantly white adipose depots and are induced (or 'recruited') when needed, such as during cold exposure. Beige adipocytes differentiate from specialized precursors, and then regress when no longer required. White adipocytes are not thermogenic, and are the major type of adipocyte found in most depots. 

Other major cell types in the fat pad include: 

Adipose stromal and progenitor cells (ASPCs). ASPCs are fibroblast-like cells that include stem cells and other adipocyte progenitors that may be in various stages of differentiation. There are also cells in the ASPC fraction that may not be progenitors themselves, but which regulate adipogenesis or provide structural support. 

Mesothelial cells. The mesothelium is a layer of epithelial cells that line the body cavities and the organs within them. Visceral fat therefore has an outer mesothelial layer, while subcutaneous adipose tissue does not. 

Vascular cells. Adipose tissue is richly vascularized, and includes arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules, and veins. The cell types found in fat include those normally found in and around the vasculature: endothelial cells of different types, smooth muscle cells, and pericytes. There is also a lymphatic vascular system in adipose tissue, characterized by specific lymphatic endothelial cells.

Immune cells. Adipose tissue contains virtually every kind of immune cell, including several types of monocytes and macrophages, B and T lymphocytes, dendritic cells, NK cells, ILCs, eosinophils, neutrophils, and basophils. 

Schwann cells. Adipose depots are innervated by both sensory and autonomic nerves. The neuronal cell bodies reside outside the fat pad in dorsal root ganglia or in sympathetic ganglia, while their axons, coated with Schwann cells, penetrate the adipose tissue.

Single cell analyses have identified many subpopulations of all of these cells in adipose tissue, and determining the lineage, molecular characteristics, and function of all of these subpopulations is a challenge current facing the field.

The cell types in adipose tissue can differ within and between depots, and can also change in response to factors like age, temperature, and nutritional status.

 

How does adipose tissue change over time? 

Adipose tissue is not static; its appearance, composition, and function change over the course of development and also in response to environmental cues. 

Adipogenesis. The process of converting a multipotent precursor cell to a mature adipocyte is called adipogenesis. This process has mostly been studied using cell culture models, but there are some data about adipogenesis in vivo. The process of developmental adipogenesis, which refers to the initial formation of the fat pad in the animal, may be somewhat different than seen in adipogenesis occurring in adult animals. 

Aging. Adipose tissue accumulates senescent cells during aging, which affect the metabolic performance of the tissue. Senescence affects multiple cell types within the fat pad, including adipocytes, ASPCs, and immune cells. 

Overnutrition. If nutrient intake is greater than energy burning, then excess calories must be stored in adipose tissue. Obesity thus occurs when there is a chronic positive imbalance in energy homeostasis. Obesity does not just affect the size and number of adipocytes, but also leads to profound changes in the immune composition of the fat pad, as generally anti-inflammatory immune cells are replaced by a pro-inflammatory portfolio of cells that contribute to the metabolic dysfunction seen in weight gain. 

Exercise. Exercise affects adipose tissue in many ways, most obviously by reducing adipose mass, but also by decreasing inflammation, promoting blood vessel formation, and altering mitochondrial activity and thermogenic potential. 

Temperature. Exposure to cold temperature has long been studied as a model for brown fat activation and beige fat biogenesis. Cold activates the sympathetic nervous system, which releases norepinephrine at specialized en passant synapses in adipose tissue, inducing a series of changes in cellular composition and gene expression.
